title: Reading f From a Graph of f′

steps.body:
Now the hardest reading of all: you are shown a graph, and told **it is f′, not f**.

Every instinct will read it as the function. Resist that.

Where the graph is **above** the axis, f is rising. Where it **crosses** the axis, f has an extremum. Where the graph is **rising**, f is concave up. The graph's HEIGHT is f's SLOPE.
Trace f′ and keep asking what f is doing.

widget.prompt: f(x) = x², and f′ is drawn beneath. Drag to where f′ = −4 — and say what f itself is doing there.
widget.successFeedback: x = −2, where f′ = −4. The lower graph is BELOW the axis, so f is falling — steeply. And the lower graph is RISING (f′ climbs from −4 toward 0), so f is concave up. Two facts about f, read entirely off the graph of f′, without ever looking at f.
widget.lowFeedback: f′ is below −4 here — even steeper downhill. Slide right.
widget.highFeedback: f′ has climbed above −4. Slide back left.

predict.prompt: At a point where the function is increasing more steeply, what should its derivative show?

options.label: The same value because height is unchanged

predict.reveal: The derivative records local slope, so a steeper upward tangent appears as a larger positive derivative value.

cml.actionGoal: Move along a function and coordinate position, local slope, and derivative graph.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: Change the controlling quantity in this derivativeTrace away from the successful state. Which invariant remains true, and which visible consequence changes?

explanation.prompt: What does the derivative graph record?

options.label: The original function's local slope at each input.
options.feedback: Exactly—this identifies the governing mechanism rather than only the final pattern.

options.label: A copy of the original function's height.
options.feedback: That describes an appearance or shortcut, not the invariant that makes the relationship hold.

options.label: The total area accumulated so far.
options.feedback: The live model contradicts that claim when its control is changed.

steps.body: A zero of f′ is an extremum of f.
explanationVariants: Where the graph of f′ CROSSES the axis from positive to negative, f stops rising and starts falling: a maximum of f.
The crossing is what matters. A graph of f′ that merely touches the axis gives a saddle of f.

widget.prompt: The graph of f′ crosses the axis from ABOVE to BELOW at x = 2. What is at x = 2 on the graph of f?

options.label: A local maximum of f.
options.feedback: Right — f was rising (f′ > 0), then falls (f′ < 0). It turned over at x = 2.

options.label: A zero of f.
options.feedback: That is what the graph would mean if it were f. But it is f′ — its zero is a FLAT SPOT of f, not a root.

options.label: An inflection point of f.
options.feedback: Inflections come from where f′ has an extremum (its own peak or valley), not where f′ crosses zero.

options.label: A local minimum of f.
options.feedback: That would need f′ to cross from BELOW to ABOVE. Here it goes the other way, so f climbs then falls.

steps.body: A peak of f′ is an inflection of f.
explanationVariants: Where f′ has a maximum, f″ = 0 and f″ changes sign — so f has an inflection. The steepest point of f is where f′ peaks.
A peak on the graph of f′ is the moment f is climbing as fast as it ever will.

widget.prompt: The graph of f′ has a MAXIMUM at x = 1 (it peaks and comes back down, staying positive). What is at x = 1 on f?

options.label: An inflection point — and the steepest climb of f.
options.feedback: Right. f′ peaking means f″ = 0 with a sign change: the bend flips, and f is climbing as fast as it ever does.

options.label: A maximum of f.
options.feedback: f′ is still POSITIVE at its own peak, so f is still climbing. A maximum of f needs f′ to reach ZERO.

options.label: A minimum of f.
options.feedback: f is rising throughout (f′ > 0). It cannot have a minimum in the middle of a climb.

options.label: A zero of f.
options.feedback: The graph shown is f′, and its shape says nothing about where f crosses the axis.

steps.body:
A translation table, worth memorising:

**f′ above the axis** → f rising.
**f′ crosses zero** → f has an extremum.
**f′ rising** → f concave up.
**f′ has a peak or valley** → f has an inflection.

Every statement about the HEIGHT of f′ is a statement about the SLOPE of f, and every statement about the SLOPE of f′ is a statement about the BEND of f.

explanationVariants: Height of f′ = slope of f. Slope of f′ = bend of f. Zero of f′ = flat spot of f.
The whole skill is refusing to read the graph as f.

widget.prompt: You are looking at a graph of f′. Match each feature to what it says about f.

pairErrors.feedback: f′ being POSITIVE means f is climbing. An extremum needs f′ to be ZERO, which happens at a crossing.
f′ RISING is a statement about the bend of f (concave up), not about its direction. Direction comes from the SIGN of f′, not its slope.

widget.missFeedback: Height of f′ = slope of f. Slope of f′ = bend of f.
widget.successFeedback: Height gives direction; slope gives bend; a crossing gives an extremum. That table is the whole skill.

hints: You are told about the graph of f′. Extrema of f come from f′ CROSSING the axis, not merely touching it.
f′ touches zero at x = 1 without crossing, and crosses at x = 4.
Only a crossing turns the curve round.
explanationVariants: f′ touches zero at x = 1 (no sign change: a saddle of f) and crosses at x = 4 (a genuine extremum). So f has exactly ONE extremum.
The touch-versus-cross distinction, one last time — it has decided the answer in every chapter of this course.

widget.prompt: A graph of f′ touches the axis at x = 1 without crossing, and crosses it at x = 4. How many EXTREMA does f have?

commonErrors.feedback: A touch is not a crossing. At x = 1 the derivative returns to the side it came from, so f does not turn — that is a saddle.
There is one: at x = 4, f′ genuinely changes sign, so f turns round.
Only two features are described, and only one of them is a sign change.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Only the crossing at x = 4 changes the sign of f′, so f has exactly one extremum.

steps.body: The height of f′ is the slope of f.
takeaways: A graph of f′ is not a graph of f. Every instinct will read it wrongly, and every instinct must be resisted.
Above the axis → f rises. Crossing the axis → f has an extremum. Rising → f is concave up.
A touch without a crossing is a saddle — the same distinction that has decided every chapter of this course.
steps.teaser: Last chapter: use all of this to find the best possible answer to a real question.

concept.body: Say it before every question: **this graph is the SLOPE of f, not f.** So its height tells you how steeply f is going, and its sign tells you which way. Where it crosses zero, f stops and turns.

explanationVariants: f′ = 3 means f is rising with slope 3. It says nothing about how high f is.
The graph of f′ carries no information at all about the VALUE of f.

widget.prompt: On the graph of f′, the height at x = 2 is 3. What does that tell you about f?

options.label: f is rising at x = 2, with slope 3.
options.feedback: Right — the height of f′ IS the slope of f.

options.label: f(2) = 3
options.feedback: That would be true if the graph were f. It is f′, so 3 is the SLOPE of f at x = 2, not its value.
